title: Batch shedding and grace-periods experiment log
body:
Purpose / short summary:

Quick experiments to evaluate the efficacy of two related levers for tail latency reduction during sustained high load: (1) lightweight batch-shedding (dropping low-utility requests from batches under load) and (2) introducing a short grace-period before flush to allow better batch formation without harming admitted latency budgets. Goal: find parameter ranges where p95/p99 improve with minimal throughput loss or increased cost.

Context / why this felt necessary:
- Recent production incidents (see INF-3241) show p99 spikes during sustained bursts even when avg latency is fine. We suspect inefficient batch composition and starvation of short requests behind long ones.
- Most prior notes focused on timeouts and max_batch_size; these experiments try a complementary approach: graceful delay (micro-grace) to increase coalescing and a shedding policy that removes requests flagged as low-utility (e.g., background embeddings or non-interactive telemetry).

Hypotheses:
1) short grace_period_ms (2-8ms) before flush will reduce p99 by 10–25% for mixed workloads by allowing one additional coalescence opportunity without increasing mean latency materially.
2) batch_shedding (evicting up to X% of oldest low-urgency requests when batch capacity is constrained) will reduce p99 for high-priority traffic at the cost of throughput for shed classes; overall system throughput should degrade <5% if shed candidates are small fraction of traffic.
3) combined approach (grace + selective shedding) yields best p99 improvements under multi-tenant pressure while maintaining throughput for high-priority requests.

Experiment setup:
- Cluster type: dedicated dev pool (4x A100-equivalent nodes), same kernel + runtime as production (v2.17.1).
- Workloads: synthetic mixed workload to emulate production mix — 60% short chat-turns (avg 30 tokens), 30% medium prompts (avg 120 tokens), 10% long-gen (avg 1024 tokens). Multipart arrival: Poisson base + superimposed microbursts (10x arrival for 500ms every 5s).
- Priority classes: HIGH (interactive), MEDIUM (batch user requests), LOW (background embedding/telemetry). LOW is shedding candidate.
- Key metrics: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, tokens/sec throughput, batch sizes distribution, fraction_shed (for shedding runs), CPU/GPU utilization, tail latency breakdowns from microtraces.
- Observability artifacts: batch_histograms, microtrace_annotated_replays, kv_cache_hit_rates, kernel_hotspots.csv. See linked_artifacts for PR and perf traces.

Parameters swept:
- max_batch_size: 8, 16, 32 (fixed)
- timeout_ms (flush): 0 (no wait), 2, 4, 8, 16
- grace_period_ms (soft wait added only when queue occupancy low-to-mid): 0, 2, 4, 8
- shedding_threshold_pct: 0%, 5%, 10%, 20% of batch capacity (only applied to LOW priority)
- starvation_protection_enabled: true/false (prevents shedding if HIGH fraction in queue > 40%)

Observations (notes by run):
- baseline (timeout=0, no grace, no shedding): clear p99 spikes during bursts; batch sizes often 1-3 for HIGH requests, medium for others. p99 ~ 420ms.
- add grace_period_ms=4 (no shedding): p99 dropped ~18% in mixed runs (420ms -> 345ms). p95 unchanged +/- 3%. Mean latency +1.5%. Rationale: extra 4ms allowed many short requests to coalesce, increasing average batch size for HIGH from 2.3 -> 4.7.
- longer grace 16ms: p99 improved further but mean latency increased ~8% and tail for short-only bursts got worse. Unacceptable tradeoff.
- shedding only (threshold 10%): p99 for HIGH improved ~22% during heavy multi-tenant bursts; fraction_shed ~4% overall since LOW class <10% of arrivals. Throughput down 2.1% (expected). Notable: shedding caused some quality-impacted logs (LOW requests missing) — acceptable for telemetry but not for production-critical customer embedding workloads.
- shedding + grace (grace=4ms, shedding=10%): best compound effect. p99 down ~30% from baseline, mean latency +2.7%. Batch sizes more stable; avg HIGH batch size 5.1. GPU utilization slightly higher but within headroom.
- starvation_protection=true: avoided pathological shedding where a sudden influx of HIGH requests would otherwise get their batches trimmed; improved safety but slightly reduced p99 gains (~2-3% relative).

Microtrace insights:
- Many p99 events were attributable to single long requests (1024 tokens) that monopolized batch processing; when grace allowed small SHORT requests to join, overall tail reduced. However, if long requests are frequent, grace simply increases queuing time and makes tails worse. So workload composition matters a lot.
- Shedding prevented low-utility long requests from clogging coalesced batches; microtraces showed reduction in queue occupancy variance and fewer outlier batches with a single very-long request.

Quantitative excerpt (median of three runs under burst profile):
- Baseline: p50 46ms, p95 180ms, p99 420ms, tokens/sec 14.8k
- Grace=4ms: p50 48ms, p95 175ms, p99 345ms, tokens/sec 15.0k
- Shedding=10%: p50 45ms, p95 160ms, p99 330ms, tokens/sec 14.5k, fraction_shed 4.0%
- Grace4 + Shedding10 + starvation_protect: p50 49ms, p95 150ms, p99 295ms, tokens/sec 14.6k, fraction_shed 3.7%

Interpretation / guidance:
- Short grace_periods (2–6ms) are a low-risk lever for mixed workloads where short interactive requests are common. They improve p99 with very small mean latency impact. Recommend opt-in default grace_ms=4 behind an SLO gate with monitoring.
- Batch_shedding is effective only when there is a clear, well-scoped low-utility class. If customers send critical embeddings in the same priority, shedding will hurt correctness. Recommend enabling shedding only for explicitly-tagged background traffic (e.g., telemetry, ad-hoc analytics) with a conservative threshold (5–10%).
- Combined approach gives multiplicative benefits but needs starvation protection to avoid demoting high-priority throughput during sudden surges.
- Important caveat: workloads dominated by long-generations ( > 512 tokens) do not benefit from grace; they get penalized. We should auto-detect composition and disable grace/shed or adjust parameters.

Implementation notes for runtime engineers:
- Grace implementation: simple per-slot soft-wait where slot open if occupancy < slot_capacity and time_since_first_enqueue < grace_ms. Implement as non-blocking sleep path on scheduler thread to avoid busy spin. Add metric: grace_coalesces_count and grace_wait_ms_histogram.
- Shedding implementation: mark candidates at admission (LOW priority) and evict LRU within batch when batch_size exceeds shedding threshold. Must emit eviction trace for debugging and customer telemetry.
- Starvation_protection: compute rolling fraction of HIGH requests in queue (100ms window); if >40%, lock shedding off for next 200ms. Tuneable constants.

Risks and open questions:
- Observability: we need finer-grained signal to detect when grace harms tail for long-heavy workloads. Propose adding workload-composition detector (ratio short:long) that toggles grace automatically.
- Edge cases: interplay with KV cache prefill and streaming responses (function-calls). Shedding a background request that had a warm KV state might be more costly than letting it through — need to check per-tenant utility.
- Customer UX: shedding implies silent drops. We should expose opt-in headers/tags and provide dropped-counter metrics to customers (and admin logs).

Next steps / TODOs:
- (Ethan) Add grace_coalesces_count and shedding_eviction_metric to exporter (INF-3307). Target PR in GH linked_artifacts.
- (Jasper) Add an adaptive-composition detector that toggles grace within Node (prototype experiment).
- (Maya) Run long-run test with production anonymized trace for 48 hours to validate steady-state effects and cost impact.
- Draft docs/console tooltip for shedding: what it does, how to tag traffic, and implications.

Conclusion:
A combination of a small grace_period and conservative shedding for explicitly-labelled low-utility traffic provides a practical path to reducing p99 without large throughput loss. Implementation should be conservative, observable, and opt-in for customers who want silent shedding. Auto-tuning based on observed composition appears promising but needs more validation.
